title: Singular Vector Finite Element Basis Functions for Tetrahedra in Complex Electromagnetic Geometries
authors: Samuel T. Elkin, Ghazi Khan, Ebrahim Forati, Brandon W. Langley, Dogan Timucin, Reza Molavi, Thomas E. Roth
abstract: Electromagnetic finite element method (FEM) implementations using traditional basis functions struggle to accurately represent field behavior near singular features such as conducting wedges. To combat this, specialized singular basis functions have been introduced to directly model the singular fields in these regions, leading to substantially improved performance. While these efforts have been pursued extensively in 2D, few functions have been developed for 3D elements. In this work, we develop basis functions for this in tetrahedra. Unlike prior functions, these basis functions are additive, meaning they are included alongside the standard vector basis functions to achieve more robust performance. Further, these functions are designed to be adaptable to tetrahedra touching several unique singular features by using combinations of basis functions singular with respect to each node and edge in the element, making them applicable to highly complex geometries. Higher-order interpolatory versions of the basis functions for modeling singular behavior with greater accuracy are also provided. These basis functions lead to substantial improvements in accuracy relative to the standard basis functions, and allow otherwise expensive simulations to be performed at far lower costs. As an application example, we perform simulations to extract critical quantities for designing superconducting qubits that significantly depend on the behavior of singular fields. In Ansys HFSS, this took 21.27 hours and a peak memory usage of 6.23 TB with 800 processors available, while using our singular basis functions achieved comparable results in 196 seconds while using 27.24 GB of memory and only 16 processors. Due to these benefits, our singular basis functions could be applied to enable design optimization of electromagnetic geometries with dominantly singular behavior, such as superconducting qubits.
summary: This paper introduces specialized singular vector finite element basis functions designed to overcome the limitations of standard FEM when simulating electromagnetic fields near sharp geometric features common in superconducting qubits. By incorporating these additive singular terms into tetrahedral elements, the authors achieve highly accurate results for critical parameters like energy participation ratios with computational costs drastically lower than commercial benchmarks.
main_problem: Traditional Finite Element Method (FEM) basis functions fail to accurately model electromagnetic field behavior near singular features, such as those found in superconducting qubit geometries.
main_result: The development of specialized, additive singular vector basis functions allows for simulating complex electromagnetic structures with massive computational speedups while maintaining high accuracy comparable to commercial solvers.
method: The authors derive and implement novel singular basis functions (node-singular, edge-singular, rotational) specifically tailored for tetrahedral elements in 3D electromagnetics.
model_or_system: The work focuses on simulating electromagnetic fields within superconducting quantum circuits, such as GCPW resonators and Xmon qubits, where energy loss near geometric singularities dictates qubit coherence times.
key_observables: Participation Ratios (PMS, PMA, PSA) quantifying energy distribution at interfaces; Quality factor (Q); Field magnitude along singular lines.
important_parameters: Singular function order ($s=1, 2, 3$); Frequency ($\omega$); Material permittivities ($\epsilon_i, \epsilon_s$).
main_assumptions: The simulation domain is assumed source-free and lossless for the primary derivations; higher-order terms require careful handling of continuity across element interfaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate field behavior comparisons (standard vs. singular functions) near wedges, show geometric associations of basis functions in tetrahedra, and compare calculated qubit parameters like capacitance and PMS against varying function orders.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the failure of standard FEM at singularities to developing node-singular, then edge-singular, and finally higher-order rotational basis functions. It validates these functions by applying them to calculate key superconducting qubit metrics (PRs, Q) and demonstrating massive computational efficiency gains over commercial tools.
why_interesting: The accurate simulation of energy loss mechanisms in superconducting qubits is crucial for understanding decoherence rates ($	ext{T}_1$, $	ext{T}_2$), which are central topics in quantum information science. The method provides a powerful, computationally efficient tool to analyze these fundamental physical limits.

Fig. 2. Examples of tetrahedra along singular features in a 3D geometry, with singular nodes and edges highlighted in red. In (a), the tetrahedron has only a single node along the conductive wedge, so only one set of node-singular functions is needed. The tetrahedron in (b) has an edge along the feature, so a set of node-singular functions is added for each node on the wedge, along with a set of edge-singular functions for that edge. A tetrahedron on a corner is shown in (c), requiring three sets of node-singular functions and two sets of edge-singular functions. The tetrahedron in (d) requires three sets of node- singular functions and one set of edge-singular functions.
